books.title: Physics Part I
books.edition: Reprint 2026-27 (first edition February 2006; revised edition November 2022; reprinted March 2024, June 2024, December 2024 and April 2026)

books.title: Physics Part II
books.edition: Reprint 2026-27 (first edition April 2006; revised edition January 2023; reprinted March 2024, June 2024, January 2025 and April 2026)

source.method: chapter titles from each book's Contents page; topics from each chapter PDF's numbered section headings (Introduction sections are not topics unless they hold a numbered subsection, as 5.1.1 and 6.1.1 do; a parent heading that is only a short lead-in to its subsections is not a separate topic; a few very short adjacent subsections are joined under one title naming them; sections listed in a chapter's opening box but absent from the chapter body are left out)

topics.title: The International System of Units
objectives: Student can distinguish base quantities and base units from derived quantities and derived units
Student can name the CGS, FPS and MKS systems and state that SI with seven base units is the accepted system today
Student can list the seven SI base quantities with their units and symbols, and the two more units, radian and steradian, defined for plane angle and solid angle
visualIdeas: a table of the seven SI base quantities, units and symbols
an arc ds on a circle of radius r showing a plane angle and a cone showing a solid angle

topics.title: Significant Figures
objectives: Student can explain significant figures as the reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit of a measurement
Student can count significant figures using the rules for zeros, decimal points and scientific notation
Student can explain why a change of units does not change the number of significant figures
visualIdeas: a reading on a scale with the reliable digits and the one uncertain digit highlighted

topics.title: Rules for Arithmetic Operations with Significant Figures
objectives: Student can apply the rule that a product or quotient keeps as many significant figures as the least precise factor
Student can apply the rule that a sum or difference keeps as many decimal places as the number with the fewest decimal places
visualIdeas: a worked density calculation with each quantity's significant figures underlined

topics.title: Rounding off the Uncertain Digits
objectives: Student can round a computed number to the required significant figures using the conventional rules
Student can apply the rule for an insignificant digit of exactly 5, raising the preceding digit only if it is odd
visualIdeas: a number line showing 2.746 rounding to 2.75 and 1.743 to 1.74

topics.title: Rules for Determining the Uncertainty in the Results of Arithmetic Calculations
objectives: Student can show how the uncertainty of measured lengths carries into a computed area
Student can explain why intermediate results in a multi-step calculation should keep one extra significant figure
visualIdeas: a rectangle with sides 16.2 +/- 0.1 cm and 10.1 +/- 0.1 cm and its area range

topics.title: Dimensions of Physical Quantities
objectives: Student can describe the dimensions of a quantity as the powers of the base quantities [M], [L], [T] and others that represent it
Student can find the dimensions of volume, velocity, acceleration and force from their definitions
visualIdeas: force broken down into mass x length / time squared with the powers shown

topics.title: Dimensional Formulae and Dimensional Equations
objectives: Student can write the dimensional formula of a physical quantity such as velocity [M0 L T-1] or density [M L-3 T0]
Student can write a dimensional equation equating a quantity with its dimensional formula
visualIdeas: a table of quantities beside their dimensional formulae

topics.title: Checking the Dimensional Consistency of Equations
objectives: Student can state the principle of homogeneity of dimensions: only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, subtracted or equated
Student can check whether an equation of motion is dimensionally consistent
Student can explain that a dimensionally correct equation need not be exactly correct, while a dimensionally wrong one must be wrong
visualIdeas: each term of x = x0 + v0t + (1/2)at^2 reduced to [L]

topics.title: Deducing Relation among the Physical Quantities
objectives: Student can use the method of dimensions to deduce how a quantity depends on up to three others, as for the period of a simple pendulum
Student can state that this method cannot give the dimensionless constants in the relation
visualIdeas: a simple pendulum with length, mass of bob and g labelled as possible variables for its period

topics.title: Instantaneous Velocity and Speed
objectives: Student can define instantaneous velocity as the limit of average velocity as the time interval tends to zero, v = dx/dt
Student can find velocity at an instant as the slope of the tangent to the position-time graph
Student can relate instantaneous speed to the magnitude of instantaneous velocity
visualIdeas: a position-time curve with secants shrinking into the tangent at t = 4 s

topics.title: Acceleration
objectives: Student can define average and instantaneous acceleration, a = dv/dt, and read it as the slope of a velocity-time graph
Student can interpret position-time and velocity-time graphs for motion with positive, negative and zero acceleration
Student can find displacement as the area under a velocity-time graph
visualIdeas: velocity-time graphs for positive, negative and zero acceleration
shaded area under a v-t graph equal to displacement

topics.title: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
objectives: Student can derive v = v0 + at, x = v0t + (1/2)at^2 and v^2 = v0^2 + 2ax using the area under the v-t graph
Student can apply the kinematic equations to problems such as free fall and stopping distance
Student can use the calculus method to obtain the same equations
visualIdeas: a v-t graph split into a rectangle and a triangle to show x = v0t + (1/2)at^2
a ball dropped from rest with positions marked at equal time intervals

topics.title: Scalars and Vectors
objectives: Student can distinguish scalar quantities (magnitude only) from vector quantities (magnitude and direction obeying the triangle law)
Student can describe position and displacement vectors and explain why displacement does not depend on the path taken
Student can state when two vectors are equal
visualIdeas: position vectors OP and OP' with the displacement vector PP'
several different paths between P and Q with the same displacement

topics.title: Multiplication of Vectors by Real Numbers
objectives: Student can describe the effect of multiplying a vector by a positive or negative real number on its magnitude and direction
Student can explain that multiplying by a dimensional scalar such as time changes the physical quantity, as velocity x time gives displacement
visualIdeas: vector A with 2A, -A and -1.5A drawn beside it

topics.title: Addition and Subtraction of Vectors - Graphical Method
objectives: Student can add vectors by the head-to-tail (triangle) method and the parallelogram method
Student can show that vector addition is commutative and associative, and describe the null vector
Student can subtract vectors as A - B = A + (-B)
visualIdeas: triangle and parallelogram constructions of A + B
A - B drawn as A + (-B)

topics.title: Resolution of Vectors
objectives: Student can express a vector as a sum of multiples of two given non-parallel vectors in a plane
Student can use unit vectors i, j, k and resolve a vector into rectangular components Ax = A cos(theta), Ay = A sin(theta)
Student can find the magnitude and direction of a vector from its components
visualIdeas: a vector resolved into x and y components on axes with unit vectors i and j

topics.title: Vector Addition - Analytical Method
objectives: Student can add vectors by adding their components, Rx = Ax + Bx and Ry = Ay + By
Student can find the magnitude and direction of the resultant of two vectors with the law of cosines and law of sines
visualIdeas: two vectors and their resultant with components added along each axis

topics.title: Motion in a Plane
objectives: Student can write the position vector r = x i + y j and the displacement of a particle moving in a plane
Student can define average and instantaneous velocity in a plane and explain that velocity is along the tangent to the path
Student can define average and instantaneous acceleration in a plane in component form
visualIdeas: a curved path with position vectors at t and t + dt and the velocity drawn tangent to it

topics.title: Motion in a Plane with Constant Acceleration
objectives: Student can write v = v0 + at and r = r0 + v0t + (1/2)at^2 for constant acceleration in a plane
Student can treat motion in a plane as two independent straight-line motions along perpendicular axes
visualIdeas: x and y motions plotted separately and combined into a curved path

topics.title: Projectile Motion
objectives: Student can describe projectile motion as uniform horizontal motion combined with uniformly accelerated vertical motion
Student can derive the parabolic path equation, time of flight, maximum height and horizontal range of a projectile
Student can show that the horizontal range is maximum for a projection angle of 45 degrees, ignoring air resistance
visualIdeas: a parabolic trajectory with velocity components drawn at several points
trajectories for different launch angles showing equal ranges for complementary angles

topics.title: Uniform Circular Motion
objectives: Student can explain why an object in uniform circular motion accelerates even though its speed is constant
Student can derive the centripetal acceleration a = v^2/R directed towards the centre
Student can relate angular speed, period and frequency to linear speed, v = R omega
visualIdeas: a particle on a circle with velocity vectors at two points and the change in velocity pointing to the centre

topics.title: Aristotle's Fallacy
objectives: Student can state Aristotle's view that a force is needed to keep a body in uniform motion
Student can explain that in practice a force is needed only to counter opposing forces such as friction
visualIdeas: a cart pushed along a road with friction opposing the push

topics.title: The Law of Inertia
objectives: Student can describe Galileo's inclined plane experiments and how he concluded that on a frictionless plane a body keeps moving with constant velocity
Student can explain inertia as the resistance of a body to a change in its state of motion
visualIdeas: a ball rolling down one smooth incline and up another, reaching the same height for smaller slopes

topics.title: Newton's First Law of Motion
objectives: Student can state Newton's first law: if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero
Student can explain everyday examples such as passengers jerking backward when a bus starts suddenly
visualIdeas: a passenger in a bus that starts suddenly, body tilting backward

topics.title: Newton's Second Law of Motion
objectives: Student can define momentum p = mv and state the second law F = dp/dt = ma, with the newton as the SI unit of force
Student can apply the second law in component form and explain why it is a local, vector law
Student can define impulse as force x time duration equal to the change in momentum and apply it to impulsive forces
visualIdeas: a cricket ball being hit back by a bat with momentum arrows before and after
a catcher drawing hands back to catch a fast ball

topics.title: Newton's Third Law of Motion
objectives: Student can state the third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
Student can explain that action and reaction act on different bodies, at the same instant, and do not cancel each other
visualIdeas: a gun and bullet with equal and opposite force arrows
a book on a table with the force pairs labelled

topics.title: Conservation of Momentum
objectives: Student can derive the conservation of total momentum of an isolated system from the second and third laws
Student can apply momentum conservation to the recoil of a gun and to collisions
visualIdeas: a gun recoiling as a bullet leaves, with momentum arrows of equal size

topics.title: Equilibrium of a Particle
objectives: Student can state that a particle is in equilibrium when the net external force on it is zero
Student can use the components of concurrent forces, or a triangle of forces, to solve equilibrium problems such as a mass hung by two strings
visualIdeas: a mass suspended by two strings with the three forces drawn as a closed triangle

topics.title: Common Forces in Mechanics
objectives: Student can distinguish gravitational force, which acts at a distance, from contact forces
Student can identify normal reaction, friction, tension and spring force as contact forces and state Hooke's law F = -kx for a spring
visualIdeas: a block on a table hung from a spring with weight, normal reaction, tension and spring force labelled

topics.title: Friction
objectives: Student can distinguish static friction, which adjusts up to a limiting value mu_s N, from kinetic friction mu_k N
Student can explain why kinetic friction is nearly independent of contact area and speed, and solve problems with blocks on inclined planes
Student can describe rolling friction and how lubricants and ball bearings reduce friction
visualIdeas: a graph of friction force rising with applied force to the limiting value then dropping to kinetic friction
a block on an incline with friction, normal force and weight components

topics.title: Circular Motion
objectives: Student can identify the centripetal force mv^2/R needed for circular motion and the forces that provide it
Student can derive the maximum safe speed of a car on a level road using static friction
Student can explain how banking a road reduces reliance on friction and find the optimum speed on a banked road
visualIdeas: a car on a level road and on a banked road with normal force and friction resolved

topics.title: Solving Problems in Mechanics
objectives: Student can choose a system and draw a free-body diagram showing all forces on it
Student can apply Newton's laws to connected bodies such as blocks joined by strings to find acceleration and tension
visualIdeas: two blocks joined by a string with separate free-body diagrams for each

topics.title: The Scalar Product
objectives: Student can define the scalar (dot) product A.B = AB cos(theta) and interpret it as one vector times the component of the other along it
Student can use the commutative and distributive laws and i.i = 1, i.j = 0 to compute dot products in component form
visualIdeas: vector A with the projection of B along it marked

topics.title: Notions of Work and Kinetic Energy: The Work-Energy Theorem
objectives: Student can derive the work-energy theorem for constant acceleration from v^2 - u^2 = 2as
Student can state that the change in kinetic energy of a particle equals the work done on it by the net force
visualIdeas: a block speeding up under a force with initial and final kinetic energies shown

topics.title: Work
objectives: Student can define the work done by a constant force as W = F.d = Fd cos(theta)
Student can explain when work done is positive, negative or zero, using examples like friction and a person holding a load
visualIdeas: a force at an angle to the displacement of a block with its component along the motion highlighted

topics.title: Kinetic Energy
objectives: Student can define kinetic energy K = (1/2)mv^2 as a scalar measure of the work a body can do by virtue of its motion
Student can compare typical kinetic energies of moving objects using the book's table
visualIdeas: a bullet, a running athlete and a car ranked by kinetic energy

topics.title: Work Done by a Variable Force
objectives: Student can find the work done by a variable force as the area under the force-displacement graph, W = integral of F dx
Student can compute work from a force-displacement graph made of simple shapes
visualIdeas: a force-displacement curve divided into thin rectangles that approach the area under the curve

topics.title: The Work-Energy Theorem for a Variable Force
objectives: Student can prove the work-energy theorem for a variable force in one dimension using dK/dt = Fv
Student can explain why the theorem is an integral form of Newton's second law
visualIdeas: kinetic energy rising as a variable force acts over a displacement

topics.title: The Concept of Potential Energy
objectives: Student can describe potential energy as stored energy due to the position or configuration of a body
Student can find the gravitational potential energy mgh of a body and relate a conservative force to the potential energy by F = -dV/dx
visualIdeas: a stretched bow-string and a ball lifted to height h

topics.title: The Conservation of Mechanical Energy
objectives: Student can state that total mechanical energy K + V stays constant when only conservative forces act
Student can define a conservative force as one whose work is path independent or zero around a closed path
Student can apply energy conservation to a body falling from a height or moving in a vertical circle
visualIdeas: bar charts of kinetic and potential energy at the top, middle and bottom of a fall

topics.title: The Potential Energy of a Spring
objectives: Student can show that the work done in stretching a spring by x is (1/2)kx^2 and that the spring force is conservative
Student can analyse a block on a spring exchanging kinetic and elastic potential energy
visualIdeas: a block attached to a spring on a smooth surface at compression, natural length and extension
parabolic potential energy curve V = (1/2)kx^2

topics.title: Power
objectives: Student can define average and instantaneous power, P = dW/dt = F.v, and use the watt and horsepower
Student can explain the kilowatt hour as a unit of energy used in electricity bills
visualIdeas: an elevator lifting a load at constant speed with force and velocity arrows

topics.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
objectives: Student can state that total linear momentum is conserved in all collisions
Student can distinguish elastic collisions, where kinetic energy is conserved, from inelastic and completely inelastic collisions
visualIdeas: two carrom coins before and after a collision

topics.title: Collisions in One Dimension
objectives: Student can find the common final velocity and kinetic energy lost in a completely inelastic collision in one dimension
Student can derive the final velocities in an elastic collision in one dimension and discuss equal masses and very unequal masses
visualIdeas: two balls on a line before and after an elastic collision, with equal masses exchanging velocities

topics.title: Collisions in Two Dimensions
objectives: Student can write momentum conservation along two axes for a collision in a plane
Student can explain why the outcome of a two-dimensional collision needs more information than the conservation laws alone
visualIdeas: a moving ball striking a stationary ball with the two outgoing directions at angles theta1 and theta2

chapters.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

topics.title: What Kind of Motion Can a Rigid Body Have?
objectives: Student can define an ideal rigid body and distinguish pure translation from rotation about a fixed axis
Student can describe rolling as a combination of translation and rotation, and precession of a spinning top as rotation about a fixed point
visualIdeas: a block sliding down an incline beside a cylinder rolling down it
a ceiling fan and a potter's wheel rotating about fixed axes

topics.title: Centre of Mass
objectives: Student can define the centre of mass of a system of particles, R = sum(m_i r_i)/M, starting from two particles on a line
Student can find the centre of mass of three particles and of uniform symmetric bodies such as a rod or a triangular lamina
visualIdeas: two masses on a line with the centre of mass closer to the heavier one
a triangular lamina with its medians meeting at the centre of mass

topics.title: Motion of Centre of Mass
objectives: Student can show that M A = F_ext: the centre of mass moves as if all the mass and all external forces were concentrated there
Student can explain why internal forces, such as in an exploding shell, do not change the motion of the centre of mass
visualIdeas: a projectile exploding mid-air while its centre of mass continues along the parabola

topics.title: Linear Momentum of a System of Particles
objectives: Student can show that the total momentum of a system is P = M V and that dP/dt = F_ext
Student can state that the total linear momentum of a system is conserved when the external force is zero, as in the radioactive decay of a moving unstable nucleus
visualIdeas: a nucleus at rest splitting into two fragments flying apart with equal and opposite momenta

topics.title: Vector Product of Two Vectors
objectives: Student can define the vector (cross) product with magnitude ab sin(theta) and direction by the right-hand rule
Student can use the properties a x b = -b x a, a x a = 0 and the cross products of unit vectors i, j, k
visualIdeas: right-hand rule with fingers curling from a to b and thumb along a x b

topics.title: Angular Velocity and its Relation with Linear Velocity
objectives: Student can describe angular velocity as a vector along the axis of rotation
Student can relate linear and angular velocity of a particle in a rotating body by v = omega x r, so v = omega r
Student can define angular acceleration alpha = d(omega)/dt
visualIdeas: a rotating disc with particles at different radii and their linear velocity arrows

topics.title: Moment of Force (Torque)
objectives: Student can define torque as tau = r x F with magnitude r F sin(theta)
Student can explain torque as the rotational analogue of force and compute it for a force applied at a distance from a pivot
visualIdeas: a spanner turning a nut with the force and perpendicular distance marked

topics.title: Angular Momentum of a Particle
objectives: Student can define angular momentum l = r x p and show that its rate of change equals the torque
Student can extend this to a system of particles: dL/dt equals the total external torque
Student can state that angular momentum is conserved when the external torque is zero
visualIdeas: a particle moving past an origin with r, p and l = r x p drawn

topics.title: Equilibrium of a Rigid Body
objectives: Student can state the conditions for translational and rotational equilibrium of a rigid body: zero net force and zero net torque
Student can describe a couple as two equal and opposite forces with different lines of action that produce rotation without translation
visualIdeas: fingers turning a bottle lid as a couple
a compass needle with equal and opposite forces at its poles

topics.title: Principle of Moments
objectives: Student can state the principle of moments for a lever in equilibrium: load arm x load = effort arm x effort
Student can explain mechanical advantage of a lever and solve balance problems with levers
visualIdeas: a lever with a fulcrum, load and effort and their arms marked

topics.title: Centre of Gravity
objectives: Student can define the centre of gravity as the point where the total gravitational torque on a body is zero
Student can explain why the centre of gravity coincides with the centre of mass in a uniform gravitational field and locate it by suspension
visualIdeas: an irregular cardboard balanced on a pencil tip and suspended from two points with plumb lines

topics.title: Moment of Inertia
objectives: Student can define moment of inertia I = sum(m_i r_i^2) as the rotational analogue of mass
Student can use the book's table of moments of inertia of a ring, disc, rod and sphere about given axes
Student can define the radius of gyration and explain the use of a flywheel
visualIdeas: a ring and a disc of equal mass with mass distribution shown relative to the axis

topics.title: Kinematics of Rotational Motion about a Fixed Axis
objectives: Student can write the equations of rotational motion with constant angular acceleration, omega = omega0 + alpha t and so on
Student can compare these equations with the kinematic equations of linear motion
visualIdeas: a table pairing linear and rotational kinematic equations

topics.title: Dynamics of Rotational Motion about a Fixed Axis
objectives: Student can derive tau = I alpha for rotation about a fixed axis
Student can find work done by a torque and rotational kinetic energy (1/2)I omega^2, and power = tau omega
visualIdeas: a flywheel driven by a cord wound on its rim

topics.title: Angular Momentum in Case of Rotation about a Fixed Axis
objectives: Student can write the angular momentum about a fixed axis as L = I omega and dL/dt = tau
Student can apply conservation of angular momentum to a girl on a swivel chair stretching out or pulling in her arms, and to an acrobat or a diver
visualIdeas: a person on a swivel chair with arms stretched out and then pulled in, spinning faster

topics.title: Kepler's Laws
objectives: Student can state Kepler's laws of orbits, areas and periods
Student can explain the law of areas as a consequence of conservation of angular momentum under a central force
visualIdeas: an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus and equal areas swept in equal times

topics.title: Universal Law of Gravitation
objectives: Student can state Newton's law of gravitation F = G m1 m2 / r^2 in vector form
Student can find the net gravitational force on a mass due to several masses by vector addition
Student can state the results for a uniform spherical shell: outside it acts as a point mass at its centre, inside the force is zero
visualIdeas: two masses with equal and opposite attraction arrows
a point mass inside and outside a spherical shell

topics.title: The Gravitational Constant
objectives: Student can describe Cavendish's torsion balance experiment to measure G
Student can state the accepted value of G, about 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2
visualIdeas: Cavendish apparatus with large and small lead spheres on a torsion wire

topics.title: Acceleration due to Gravity of the Earth
objectives: Student can derive g = G M_E / R_E^2 by treating the earth as concentric spherical shells
Student can use g to estimate the mass of the earth
visualIdeas: the earth drawn as concentric shells with a mass on its surface

topics.title: Acceleration due to Gravity below and above the Surface of Earth
objectives: Student can derive how g decreases with height h, approximately g(1 - 2h/R_E) for small h
Student can derive how g decreases with depth d, g(1 - d/R_E), and explain why g is greatest at the earth's surface
visualIdeas: a graph of g against distance from the earth's centre rising linearly inside and falling as 1/r^2 outside

topics.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
objectives: Student can find the work done in lifting a mass near the earth's surface as mg(h2 - h1)
Student can derive the gravitational potential energy -G M_E m / r with zero at infinity
Student can define gravitational potential as potential energy per unit mass
visualIdeas: a curve of gravitational potential energy against distance, negative and rising towards zero at infinity

topics.title: Escape Speed
objectives: Student can derive the escape speed from the earth, v = sqrt(2 g R_E), about 11.2 km/s
Student can explain why the moon has no atmosphere using its low escape speed
visualIdeas: a rocket launched at different speeds: falling back, orbiting and escaping

topics.title: Earth Satellites
objectives: Student can derive the orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit and its period
Student can relate the period of a satellite to its orbital radius as in Kepler's third law
visualIdeas: a satellite in a circular orbit with gravity providing the centripetal force

topics.title: Energy of an Orbiting Satellite
objectives: Student can show that a satellite in a circular orbit has kinetic energy G M m / 2r and total energy -G M m / 2r
Student can explain why the negative total energy means the satellite is bound to the earth
visualIdeas: bar chart of kinetic, potential and total energy of an orbiting satellite

topics.title: Stress and Strain
objectives: Student can define stress as restoring force per unit area and strain as fractional change in dimension
Student can distinguish tensile (or compressive), shearing and hydraulic stress and the corresponding longitudinal, shearing and volume strain
visualIdeas: a cylinder under tensile, shearing and hydraulic stress side by side

topics.title: Hooke's Law
objectives: Student can state Hooke's law: for small deformations stress is proportional to strain
Student can identify the proportionality constant as the modulus of elasticity
visualIdeas: a straight-line stress-strain graph for small deformation

topics.title: Stress-Strain Curve
objectives: Student can describe the stress-strain curve of a metal: proportional limit, yield point, elastic and plastic regions, ultimate tensile strength and fracture
Student can distinguish ductile and brittle materials, and elastomers that do not obey Hooke's law
visualIdeas: a labelled stress-strain curve of a metal
stress-strain curve of rubber-like elastic tissue

topics.title: Young's Modulus
objectives: Student can define Young's modulus as tensile (or compressive) stress divided by longitudinal strain, Y = (F/A)/(dL/L)
Student can calculate the extension of a wire or rod using Young's modulus
Student can explain why steel is preferred in heavy-duty machines using its higher Young's modulus
visualIdeas: a loaded wire stretching with its original length and extension marked

topics.title: Shear Modulus
objectives: Student can define shear modulus (modulus of rigidity) G = shearing stress / shearing strain
Student can calculate the sideways displacement of a block under a shearing force
visualIdeas: a block with its top face pushed sideways by a tangential force

topics.title: Bulk Modulus
objectives: Student can define bulk modulus B = -p/(dV/V) and compressibility as its reciprocal
Student can compare bulk moduli of solids, liquids and gases
visualIdeas: a cube shrinking uniformly when submerged under hydraulic pressure

topics.title: Poisson's Ratio
objectives: Student can define lateral strain and Poisson's ratio as lateral strain divided by longitudinal strain
Student can explain why Poisson's ratio has no units
visualIdeas: a wire stretching longer and thinner with both changes marked

topics.title: Elastic Potential Energy in a Stretched Wire
objectives: Student can derive the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire, (1/2) x stress x strain x volume
Student can calculate the energy stored per unit volume of a stretched wire
visualIdeas: area under the force-extension line representing stored energy

topics.title: Applications of Elastic Behaviour of Materials
objectives: Student can explain how elastic properties guide the design of crane ropes, beams and columns
Student can explain from the sag of a loaded beam why increasing its depth reduces bending more than increasing its breadth, and why a mountain on earth can be only about 10 km high
visualIdeas: a crane lifting a load with a thick steel rope
a beam supported near its ends and loaded at the centre, sagging

topics.title: Pressure
objectives: Student can define pressure as normal force per unit area and use the pascal as its SI unit
Student can explain everyday observations such as a sharp needle piercing skin using pressure
Student can define density and relative density of a fluid
visualIdeas: a blunt spoon and a sharp needle pressed with the same force on skin

topics.title: Pascal's Law
objectives: Student can state Pascal's law that pressure in a fluid at rest is the same at all points at the same height
Student can explain why the pressure at a point in a fluid acts equally in all directions
visualIdeas: a small prism-shaped fluid element with equal pressures on its faces

topics.title: Variation of Pressure with Depth
objectives: Student can derive P = Pa + rho g h for a fluid at rest
Student can explain the hydrostatic paradox: pressure depends on depth, not on the shape of the vessel
visualIdeas: vessels of different shapes filled to the same height showing equal pressure at the base

topics.title: Atmospheric Pressure and Gauge Pressure
objectives: Student can describe the mercury barometer and the value of atmospheric pressure at sea level
Student can distinguish gauge pressure from absolute pressure and read an open-tube manometer
visualIdeas: Torricelli's mercury barometer with a 76 cm column
an open-tube manometer

topics.title: Hydraulic Machines
objectives: Student can state that a change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished
Student can explain how a hydraulic lift and hydraulic brakes multiply force
visualIdeas: a hydraulic lift with a small piston and a large piston carrying a car

topics.title: Streamline Flow
objectives: Student can describe steady (streamline) flow and turbulent flow
Student can derive the equation of continuity A v = constant for an incompressible fluid
visualIdeas: streamlines crowding together where a pipe narrows

topics.title: Bernoulli's Principle
objectives: Student can derive Bernoulli's equation P + (1/2)rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline from work and energy
Student can state the assumptions of Bernoulli's principle and apply it to fluid at rest
visualIdeas: a pipe rising and narrowing with pressure, speed and height marked at two sections

topics.title: Speed of Efflux: Torricelli's Law
objectives: Student can derive the speed of efflux from a hole in a tank, v = sqrt(2 g h) for an open tank
Student can explain that this speed equals that of a body falling freely through the same height
visualIdeas: water jets from a hole near the bottom of a tank

topics.title: Dynamic Lift
objectives: Student can explain dynamic lift on a spinning ball (Magnus effect) using Bernoulli's principle
Student can explain the lift on an aerofoil from the faster flow above the wing
visualIdeas: streamlines around an aircraft wing
a spinning ball with air flow faster on one side

topics.title: Viscosity
objectives: Student can describe viscosity as internal friction between fluid layers in relative motion
Student can define the coefficient of viscosity as shearing stress divided by strain rate and explain its variation with temperature
visualIdeas: layers of liquid flowing in a pipe with the speed largest at the centre

topics.title: Stokes' Law
objectives: Student can state Stokes' law for the viscous drag on a sphere, F = 6 pi eta a v
Student can derive the terminal velocity of a sphere falling through a viscous fluid
